::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Complex Numbers : Proof](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2069778/complex-numbers-proof), asked by [Oran2013](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/400083/oran2013) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2016-12-23; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> Prove that if $w,z$ are complex numbers such that $|w|=|z|=1$ and $wz\ne -1$, then $\frac{w+z}{1+wz}$ is a real number.
>
> Do I substitute $w$ and $z$ for $a+bi$ and $c+di?$ How do I do this?
:::

Breaking it down into components $w = a+bi$ and $z=c+di$ is going to be extremely tedious.  Like Fib1123 says, you want to show that $\frac{w+z}{1+wz}$ is its own conjugate.  In general,
$$\overline{\frac{w+z}{1 + wz}} = \frac{\bar w+ \bar z}{1 + \bar w \bar z}$$
Now multiply by $1=\frac{wz}{wz}$ and use the fact that 
$$|w| = w \bar w = |z| = z \bar z = 1$$
